segments.note: Kentucky's first railroad, the Lexington and Ohio, reached Frankfort in 1834 but stalled there after the Panic of 1837 and was seized by the state in 1840. The Louisville and Frankfort Railroad, organized 1847, built east from Louisville (through La Grange, then Eminence, Pleasureville, and Bagdad in Shelby/Henry/Franklin counties) and completed its Kentucky River bridge into Frankfort in August 1851; in 1852 it connected with the rebuilt Lexington and Frankfort Railroad (successor to the L&O's Lexington-Frankfort trackage), giving through Louisville-Frankfort-Lexington service for the first time via twice-daily trains. The two companies unified operations Jan 1 1857 while remaining separate corporations until 1869. Frequency for this era is estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: The Lexington and Frankfort and Louisville and Frankfort railroads formally merged in September 1869 to form the Louisville, Cincinnati and Lexington Railroad (the 'Cincinnati' in the name came from the separate 1869-72 Short Line cutoff to Covington/Cincinnati, which diverged from this Frankfort-Lexington route near Anchorage east of Louisville; see ln_louisville_cincinnati.geojson). LC&L trains left Frankfort at 9:20 a.m. and 5:50 p.m. for Lexington, and at 7:08 a.m. and 3:33 p.m. for Louisville - two round trips daily.

segments.note: By 1893 the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway began operating its own passenger trains over this L&N branch under trackage rights, roughly doubling service as the line carried both L&N locals and C&O through trains between the Bluegrass and Louisville. Aggregate frequency for this era is estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: By the 1950s-60s the corridor's passenger service had narrowed to a single daily round trip: the C&O's George Washington, a flagship Pullman train running Newport News-Cincinnati-Louisville via Frankfort and Lexington. It made its final call at Frankfort April 30, 1971, the day before Amtrak's May 1 launch; Amtrak never picked up this route, and unlike most lines in this dataset, no passenger train has run between Louisville and Lexington since. Today the corridor survives only for freight: CSX (as the unnamed western end of its network near Anchorage/La Grange Junction) and R.J. Corman's Central Kentucky Lines (Frankfort to Lexington).
